title: The bell-stand maker
hook: Woodworker Qing fasts until he forgets praise and reward, then carves (Zhuangzi 19)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chop wood: Layman Pang's marvelous activity was carrying water and hauling firewood. Your line was fully present to the weight of the bucket. Today, a woodworker from an old Chinese book.
screen: `FULLY PRESENT TO THE WEIGHT OF THE BUCKET.`

segments.voice: A wooden stand for hanging bells, finished and set out where people can see it. In the story, everyone who looks at it is startled. It seems too good for human hands, as if spirits made it. The ruler of Lu sees it too, and he questions the woodworker, a man named Qing. What technique? What training? What trick? Qing's answer, in the Chinese book called the Zhuangzi, isn't about chisels at all. It's about what he had to forget before he picked one up. Today's word is the craftsman himself: Qing.
screen: `TOO GOOD FOR HUMAN HANDS.` → `THE RULER WANTS THE SECRET.` → `IT ISN'T ABOUT CHISELS.`

segments.voice: First, the answer begins humbly. Qing says, in paraphrase, I'm only a workman, what art could I have? But there is one thing. Before he makes a bell-stand, he fasts, to make his mind still. Second, what the fast takes away. After three days, the text says, he no longer thinks of congratulations, reward, rank or pay. After five days, he no longer thinks of praise or blame, of being skillful or clumsy. After seven days, he forgets even his own limbs and body, and the ruler's court has dropped out of his mind. Notice the order: first the paycheck, then the audience, then the self who wanted both. Third, what's left. Only then does Qing walk into the forest. He looks at the trees, at their natural shape, until he finds one where he can already see the bell-stand inside it. Then he sets his hand to it. If he can't see it, he leaves the tree alone. The Zhuangzi calls this, in paraphrase, heaven meeting heaven: what's natural in the worker meeting what's natural in the wood. Fourth, why this still speaks to a modern desk. Work can come with a prize always in view: the likes, the raise. Qing's story doesn't say rewards are evil. It says they get in the way of seeing. Work done while watching the audience is done half-looking. The bell-stand that startled everyone came from someone who, for a while, had stopped caring whether it would.
screen: `I'M ONLY A WORKMAN.` · `PAY, THEN PRAISE, THEN SELF.` · `HE SEES IT IN THE TREE.` · `ONE EYE ON THE PRIZE.` · then, large: `THE BELL-STAND MAKER.`

segments.voice: Hold a piece of work ahead of you today and, like Qing, set things down one at a time: first what you'll get for it, then what people will say about it, then even the worry about whether you're good enough. What's left is the task itself and the material in front of you; rest there. If you pray, you can bring the work in your own tradition's words.
Qing. The woodworker in the Zhuangzi who fasted until he forgot reward and praise, then saw the bell-stand inside the tree. Today's word.
Your line: forget the prize. What's left is the work, and the wood. That's day nine hundred one.

howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi, including Daoist teachers and students of Chinese philosophy, often turn to Qing's story when talking about craft, focus and working without attachment to reward.

chat.says: How did that woodworker in the Zhuangzi make a bell-stand so good it looked magical?
options: He fasted until he forgot reward, praise and self, then found the stand already in a tree.
He trained for decades on a secret chiseling technique handed down in his family.
The ruler promised him a huge reward, so he worked harder than anyone else.
chat.meaning: Qing says his only art is fasting until pay, praise and even his body drop away; then he sees the bell-stand in the tree.

Zhuangzi.meaning: an old Chinese book where Qing's story is told

Qing.meaning: the woodworker who made the bell-stand

Lu.meaning: an old Chinese state; its ruler questions Qing

sources.ref: Zhuangzi, chapter 19 (Da Sheng), the woodworker Qing

notes: Zhuangzi 19 paraphrased throughout (Legge 1891 renders the name Khing). The three, five and seven days of fasting and what is forgotten at each stage come from the text; confirm against Legge.
'Heaven meeting heaven' paraphrases the story's closing phrase; confirm.
Trapdoor third floor names chapter 19 as 'the chapter on understanding life' (Da Sheng / 'The Full Understanding of Life' in Legge); confirm title phrasing.
The ruler is called 'the ruler of Lu' (Legge: the Marquis of Lu).
